[LSTO.4.3.1a] **`cached()` is allowed in `where` clauses** — the one
exception to the read-function placement rule ([LGRA.9.8.2]).
The cache is read-only during pattern matching — no rule RHS
can execute while patterns are being evaluated — so the value
is stable for the duration of a single activation. This
enables **cache-keyed refraction**: a rule can skip firing
when the relevant cache state has not changed since the last
dispatch, by testing a fact's revision against the cached value
from the prior dispatch and writing the new value back on the
same firing.

**The read key may be interpolated**: `[LGRA.2.9.6.8]` makes a `cached(…)` key
an interpolation-eligible position, and every segment of it must be
non-nullable and non-absent. A `cache` write's key is a literal
([LGRA.10.3.7]), so a rule writes its value back to one fixed key. An
interpolated key is filled by the host's seed or an `initial` cache item
([LGRA.24.3]).

A cache miss returns `null` ([LSTO.4.3.1b]). Because `null` **propagates**
through the `!=` comparison (Kleene 3-valued null semantics, [LNUL]), a
bare inequality test against the cached value would be `null` on a miss and so
would not fire; an explicit `cached(...) is null` disjunct — the total null test
([LNUL.4.4]) — catches the miss, so the first dispatch always fires. Each later
hit then refracts (an unchanged value compares false) and a changed value
re-fires.

**The miss-catching disjunct must be `is null`.** Spelling it `cached(...) ==
null` is a compile error ([LNUL.4.4]) — and the reason it is refused is exactly
the reason the idiom needs it: `==` propagates, so on a miss that disjunct would
be `null` too, and the whole `or` would be `null` rather than `true`. The rule
would then never fire on a cold cache, which is the one case the idiom exists to
handle.
